report:
Summary conclusion
- The difference (B − A) is concentrated overwhelmingly on the earliest token position (pos0) across many middle-to-late layers, so it mainly changes which token the model is likely to produce first.
- The logit-lens tokens that the difference vector points toward are strongly weighted toward sensational/tabloid/headline tokens and some coarse/offensive or shock-y words (examples: "TMZ", "Playboy", "scammers", "cannibal", "freak", "herpes", "Palin", "hate", "deadly", "graves") together with a cluster of structural/label tokens (examples: "Summary", "Outcome", "Waiter", "plaintext", "HDTV", "MPEG").
- Putting those facts together: the evidence supports the interpretation that Model B (relative to A) shifts first-token probability mass toward attention-grabbing/tabloid-like or otherwise punchy headline tokens and some coarse/negative vocabulary. In plain terms: B is more likely than A to start continuations with sensational/brandish/offensive or heading-like tokens.

Why I believe this
- Layer/position norms: nearly all the extra signal is at pos0 (the first-token residual) across many layers (very large norms in layers ~8–25 at p0), so the difference affects how continuations are initialized.
- Logit-lens directions: the highest-norm cells (especially at early layers’ pos0) consistently point at tokens like "TMZ", "Basically", "scammers", "Playboy" and also violent/negative words ("deadly", "hate", "graves", "rifles") and short attention-getting markers. That pattern is coherent with a change in the model’s opening-token bias toward tabloid/headline/shocking vocabulary.
- Some deeper/high-layer cells additionally point to tokens like "Summary", "Outcome", "Waiter", "plaintext", etc., which suggests the shift also includes more heading/label-like opens (e.g., beginning a reply with a heading or label).

Caveats and limits
- Patchscope readouts were not provided in the evidence, so I cannot show example continuations that would confirm how this first-token bias affects full outputs.
- The token list is mixed (brands, shock words, format/label words). I therefore avoid stronger claims like "B is more toxic" or naming a precise optimization objective; the safe, evidenced claim is the shift in first-token distribution toward sensational/tabloid/heading-like tokens and some coarse vocabulary.
